articles.text: Piedmont’s school board officially ratified teacher contract at the June 12 meeting. Piedmont School District and the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) are now in agreement with teacher salary raises in place for the current school year and the next two years. “I’m going to be short on comments, but very large on regard for our APT members. This, as we know, is a year in the making, and we have finally arrived,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Board members were also brief with their comments, two and half hours into the penultimate meeting of the school year. No public comment was made and no comments were made by teacher union representatives. “The three year agreement means that we can really focus on all the things that we want to come together and collaborate on for the next few years. So a huge thanks to the negotiating teams. This is exciting,” said Board Vice President Lindsay Thomasson. Board member Cory Smegal eagerly jumped at the chance to present a motion for the agenda item, setting the stage for the unanimous 5-0 vote approving the agreement. Teachers secured a 3% retroactive raise to salaries for this past year, 4% next year and 4.5% in 2025-26. The final year’s raise would only be 3% if the increase to Measure H, one of two school parcel taxes, does not pass in the upcoming November election. Piedmont teachers, shown at graduation, wore many hats this year as educators, coaches, mentors and negotiators.
articles.title: Teacher contract finalized

A debate that needs to end By Pastor Jim Hopkins Every once in a while I need to explain to someone that yes, I serve a Baptist congregation, that yes we are proud of that identity, and yes we are quite different from the largest Baptist, and largest Protestant denomination in the United States, the Southern Baptist Convention. The Baptist tradition in the United States has always been quite diverse in terms of theology, culture, worship style, racial/ethnic identity, emphasis in ministry, etc. (The first Baptist Church in the colonies was the First Baptist Church in America, founded by Roger Williams in Providence, Rhode Island in 1638. That congregation is still active.) What defined the Baptist tradition was an emphasis on what historian Walter Shurden calls the four fragile freedoms: Soul Freedom, Bible Freedom, Church Freedom and Religious Freedom. The Southern Baptist Convention was founded in 1845 when it separated from other Baptists over the issue of slavery. It included the American Baptist Home Mission Society, the precursor of the American Baptist Churches USA to which the congregation I serve belongs. Most precisely the Baptist Foreign Mission Board denied a request by the Alabama Convention that enslavers be eligible to become missionaries. The Southern Baptist Convention was formed in protest. Currently, the Southern Baptist Convention is frequently in the news over its refusal to support women as ordained ministers. Many of its congregations have been forced out for ordaining, hiring and supporting women in pastoral roles. In May, one of the founding churches of the convention, the First Baptist Church of Richmond, Virginia, voted to sever ties with the SBC rather than fire a female pastor. While no congregation, including Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, can claim that it has supported women in ministry without failure or fault, we were one of the first American Baptist congregations to ordain (1972) and hire women. While there are scattered verses in the Bible that can be marshalled against women in pastoral roles, there are many verses and examples that are supportive of the same. articles.text: Move signals decline of camphor trees in Piedmont Citing its ill health and declining state, the Piedmont Public Works Department removed a “prominent” camphor (cinnamomum campora) street tree near the corner of Guilford and Highland Avenues on Tuesday, June 11. Though popular, most of the city’s camphor trees are in different stages of decline, according to the Public Works Department. The removal of this tree is part of the city’s plans to move away from using camphor trees in the near future. “It is sad because it is a really prominent tree,” said Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent at a Park Commission meeting earlier this month. Camphor trees are commonly seen on Piedmont’s streets. A total of 90 are maintained by the City of Piedmont on Ronada Avenue, Ramona Avenue, York Drive, Grand Avenue, Cambridge Way, Highland and Indian Avenue. Though prominent, this camphor tree on Highland Avenue had been in poor health for a decade. In her presentation at the Park Commission Meeting on June 5, Kent described the tree as “totally dead,” and used a series of Google Earth images to show that it had been slowly deteriorating since 2020. Resident Richard Nagler, who lives near Hazel Lane, confirmed her reports. “It was a tree that was clearly dead. I’d been kind of watching that tree for months and months and months, waiting to see what was going to happen,” said Nagler. He recalled that he and his wife would often have conversations about it, wondering if a branch would fall or if the tree itself might fall someday. In general, if a tree is in decline but safe, the City will usually leave it in place until there are signs of structural concerns. At the Park Commission Meeting, Kent explained that on the whole, camphor trees in Piedmont are in a state of decline. “They are at the height of their mature level and at various levels of [...] fair to poor condition,” she explained. Of the total 90 camphor trees, she reported that 36 were in “good” condition, 47 were “fair,” six were “poor,” and one was in “critical.” “We’re going to have to start replacing a lot of the camphors in the city, and we will not be replanting with camphors,” she declared. “There are a lot of issues with them [...] over time, these camphors are going to leave our urban forest.” Park Commission member David Johnson acknowledged that the tree is one many cities in California have started to transition away from, but urged the City to “think of keeping some in parks or open spaces where they have lots of room to grow.” Nagler witnessed the tree’s removal on Tuesday, June 11, as he was walking down Highland Avenue. “It was just three guys from Public Works working very quietly, meticulously, taking down this big tree. One guy up in the tree, two guys on the ground guiding him. It’s pretty extraordinary that our Public Works department could handle a project that big. It was very impressive to see how carefully and thoroughly they were working,” he said. Nagler suggested that this particular space on Highland Avenue could do without a tree for now. “Maybe it’ll give the cars going in and out of Guilford a little bit more visibility.” For more information about street trees and the city’s future plans, please contact Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager, by phone at (510) 420-3064 or by email at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Staff photo Piedmont Community Service Crew members Asha Byers (left), Jessica Liu and Simran Titan serve pancakes, sausages and fruit to attendees of the annual pancake breakfast on July 4. Piedmont’s annual Pancake Breakfast will return to the Veterans Hall this year as part of the city’s Fourth of July Parade festivities. The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a coed Piedmont Scout Venturing unit, will serve a nourishing breakfast from 8:00 to 10:30 a.m. with pancakes, sausages, fresh fruit and coffee. “It is a longstanding Piedmont tradition that old-timers and sometimes newcomers look forward to,” said Ken Li, crew advisor for the PCSC. “It’s got great community spirit and PCSC has been fortunate to take it over.” The Pancake Breakfast is one of the city’s most anticipated events of the year. The Piedmont-Montclair Rotary Club operated it for many years after inheriting it from the Fire Department. The Piedmont Recreation Department operated it for some years, then handed it over the tradition to the PCSC in 2015, which has carried it on ever since. This will be the PCSC’s sixth year in charge of the event. In addition to its popularity, the Pancake Breakfast is one of the PCSC’s largest fundraising events. Every year, crew members sign up to volunteer at the breakfast, set up the dining area, cook, prep-cook (including slicing fruit and making pancake batter), serve food and drinks, keep the dining area clean during operations and finally store the organization’s kitchen supplies until the following year. “Every year there’s a classic marketing question,” said Li. Will the attendance or the community support be smaller or bigger than last year?” The event typically attracts about 400 people, but Li expects that number will be even higher this year. “One of the things I challenged our crew members on was to do more marketing and see if that can push up our attendance,” he said. “The money we raise is not for the crew members. It’s for the philanthropy that we do – building tiny houses, cooking for the food insecure. That’s where you can see our funding at work,” he explained. The Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-led venturing crew under the auspices of Piedmont Scout Council, inspiring teenagers to actively uplift the broader community through service projects. For more information and to learn how you can help or join, visit pcservicecrew. org/new-member and contact crew advisor Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@ sbcglobal.net. The Pancake Breakfast will take place at Veteran’s Hall on Thursday, July 4 from 8:00 to 10:30 a.m. Tickets to the pancake breakfast are $15 per person. They will accept both cash and PayPal as payment.

articles.text: The Barrelhouse Jazz Band has been playing traditional (Dixieland) jazz in the Bay Area since 1972. Like the earliest traditions of jazz music, the Barrelhouse boys sprang from a church. More than 50 years ago, a small group of musicians at Montclair Presbyterian Church formed a traditional jazz band. The band’s focus remains the West Coast brand of New Orleans-style jazz developed by San Francisco musician Lu Watters using a two-trumpet sound. The band loves to see people dancing to its music, something that brings out the best in the Barrelhouse musicians. The band often plays for church services in several denominations in the Bay Area, providing much joy among the parishioners. In addition to playing swing music and fox-trots for dance music, the band plays struts, stomps, blues and rags. The current band members are director Al Flood (clarinet & sax), Virginia Tichenor (piano), Jim Klippert (trombone), Bruce Stangeland (banjo), Art Wood (trumpet), David Auerbach (tuba) and Scott Wild (drums). articles.text: Photo by Rob Peterson Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team put girls’ sports on center stage on September 30, 2022 by hosting the school’s Homecoming game for the first time in a year when the football game was canceled. In the photo Bauer Peterson sets Bree DeYoung (3) for a spike. It was a time to celebrate another Piedmont sports achievement at the school board meeting on June 12. Piedmont’s Title IX Task Force celebrated not a win, but a tie, with the announcement that Piedmont High School had an equal number of boys and girls playing on sports teams. A participation gap by gender was formally first addressed by conducting an interest survey in Spring 2022 among 8th-12th graders. This led to the offer of girls’ beach volleyball in 2022-23. The survey also showed that girls would enjoy playing flag football if offered as a varsity team. The State added flag football as a varsity sport for girls the following year, and PHS athletes responded with 41 girls signing up this past fall, requiring two teams. Title IX coordinator, and district Director of Instructional Technology, Stephanie Griffin, who not incidentally was the high school’s first Girl’s Athletic Director, reported to the board on the year end progress of gender equity in sports. “We’re a model when it comes to Title IX. It’s something for our community to be proud of,” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. The Title IX Task Force officially was created by former PHS Principal Adam Littlefield in the Spring of 2022. Two experts also helped support the task force, Dr. Donna Lopiano, CEO of Women’s Sports Foundation for 15 years, and former Alameda County Deputy District Attorney Kim Hunter, a Piedmont resident. Parents Molly Lloyd and Kim DeYoung repeatedly spoke at the board meetings, gathered data on their own and advocated publicly for the participation of more sports for girls. “Prior to [the taskforce] there was a huge amount of effort by parents in the district trying to get the attention of administration to actually do this work,” said school board member Cory Smegal. In addition to the participation gap, Griffin and Dolowich spoke about specific issues the Title 9 effort has faced affecting the qualitative experience of athletes. “Over the last couple of years we have observed several disparities in those experiences along gender lines- maybe in competition, in uniforms and equipment, practice times, etc. Addressing these sorts of issue is very operational it’s in the trenches with the director of athletics and the school administration,” said Griffin. Newly hired Athletic Director Tyler Small was on hand at the meeting to show support for the effort of the Task Force. “This is like a present, gift wrapped for your desk [as you arrive],” said School Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen to Small. The task force also looked at the intangibles from participating in sports and did so with the methodology of Lopiano. When the task force was formed in 2022, 15 of 48 categories were determined to be an advantage for boys, only one for girls. Two years later, there are now 11 areas of benefits advantaged towards girls sports. “Obviously we are not done; we have an action plan and Tyler’s got some more work to do. He’s ready and fired up for that. But you guys have laid the groundwork for how we are going to measure this,” said Smegal.

articles.text: You can turn a gathering around the campfire into a perfect summer science lesson with this activity. We are putting a twist on the classic s’mores snack by packing marshmallows, chocolate and more into waffle cones for the ultimate summer treat. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that began as solid ingredients begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey. Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore, acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science. Materials: • Waffle cones • Mini marshmallows • Chocolate • Graham crackers • Your choice of toppings, chopped into small pieces - Chocolate candies, candy bars, nuts, sprinkles, popcorn, Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. • • • peanut butter cups, coconut, fresh fruit, etc. Foil Camp fire or oven Bowls for toppings Procedure: 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice! 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using the oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. What do you think is happening on the inside of the waffle cones? d. How might the fire change them? Do you think it’s similar or different to the marshmallow earlier? 7. Once they’re done cooking, remove them from the heat and let cool for about a minute. 8. Carefully remove from the foil and make some observations of your results: a. Does it look the same or different from how it was before? b. What do you notice about it now? c. Where else have you seen something melt like this in the kitchen? What other ingredients melt and become gooey like marshmallows do? 9. Finally, enjoy the results of your experiment! Find more activities and at-home exper i ment s on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Be sure to share your observations with us on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter @chabotspace. Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills.

Rogue Retreat offers a broad array of services including temporary housing, recovery programs for unhoused people with past trauma and substance abuse issues and community food programs that make reintegrating into the community easier for unhoused people. PCSC also partnered with Rogue Retreat last year. During their trip, volunteers from PCSC were tasked with repairing and improving homes in Rogue Retreat’s 150-person tiny house village. In specific, the team was tasked with building entry stairs for 19 of the site’s duplex homes as well as repainting them. When they weren’t working on the houses, the crew was serving food to its inhabitants at the site’s kitchen. “While we were working, we could see the residents coming and going, and some of them would talk to us,” said Li. He described the experience as “insightful” and “heartwarming” for many of the volunteers. Volunteer Bryson Cheney agreed. “We got to interact a lot more with the people we were helping, see our work come together and have an impact day by day. With a lot of other projects, we don’t often see the full impact of our work or get to meet those that we help. That was a nice change and motivator,” he recalled. At night, the crew stayed with local host family David Nilson (a professional colleague and friend of Ken Li), Leslie Nilson (David’s wife) and Julie Madiarmid (David’s sister). Between serving local communities, the crew also made some time for some fun excursions into Oregon and Northern California. The students went whitewater rafting on the Smith River, hiked through Redwoods in the Ashland area and visited Rogue Creamery, a cheesemaker whose claim to fame involves serving its cheese to French President Emmanuel Macron in 2022. Harry McNulty and Shou Presley greet one of the Billy goats at WillowWitt farm. articles.text: Qatar Airways is one of the most awarded and prestigious airways in the world. With over 18,000 “excellent” ratings on Trip Advisor and proud winner of the Travelers Choice award from 2017-2020. It turned out to be one of the worst flight experiences for my family. We took two flights – a 15-hour flight from SFO to Doha and another one clocking in at approximately five hours to Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia. Qatar Air had come highly recommended to us from my uncle, who frequently flew with them and often raved about it. I’m sure anyone who has ever sat in economy will tell you how uncomfortable the chairs are, how little legroom there is or the strange mush of substance the airline calls ‘food’. The oxblood colored seats were almost entirely devoid of cushioning, and all three meals tasted off. Overall, it was an extremely disappointing experience. On top of this, chairs were packed together tighter than any other airline I’ve flown. Why would my uncle not stop bragging about this airline when my family swore to never fly it again? For starters my uncle, recently retired, flew mostly for business, sitting in business and occasionally first class. Qatar Airways is constantly celebrated for its decadent business class along with the luxurious cabins, spacious bathrooms and gourmet meals that come with shelling out up to ten times more on a seat. While our flight was uncomfortable and led to irritation, it was, overall, a rather small thing in the grand scheme of it all. But it’s not a small thing. The portrayal of Qatar as a first-class airline and often overlooking portrayal of economy class in advertisements is harmful to many. Qatar isn’t the only airline or service or product to do this. In fact, portraying the best parts of something is the goal for marketers alike whether it’s for an air fryer or trendy restaurant. By adapting more transparency as a marketing norm, companies can build and foster trust between themselves and their customers. My family didn’t book economy class then walk on the plane and expect a gourmet filet mignon and fully reclining seats. We did, however, hold Qatar to a higher standard, excited to see why it was so highly praised. Qatar Airways is not alone in the struggle of preferential marketing. It’s universal and has existed since probably the Dark Ages. This is precisely why it needs to be changed. By embracing transparency, companies can bridge the gap of customer expectations to build lasting trust and loyalty. While it is important to showcase the strengths of a corporation and its goods, it is equally important to show a diverse, inclusive range. My experience is an opportunity to call for improvement. Industries must reflect on their image and communication to spot flaws and strive for truthful portrayals of their services. Until this notion has been accepted as a norm, we cannot achieve truly beneficial consumer-producer relationships. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen who frequently writes for The Post.

articles.text: Tournament bracket for Copa America 2024 soccer tournament Summer soccer is here! Copa América officially returns this week with Argentina and Canada getting things started on tomorrow, June 20 at 5:00 p.m. Provided is how each group shapes up, each team’s FIFA ranking, and our final predictions of how the tournament plays out. We’ll start with the United States’ Group C and go from there. Group C: No. 11 USA, No. 15 Uruguay, No. 45 Panama, No. 85 Bolivia The United States walks into Group C in an inconsistent run of form, giving fans some uneasiness entering Copa America. They recently lost to Colombia 5-1 on June 8 but tied 1-1 with tournament favorites Brazil on June 12. Regardless, they should be the favorites to take the group, which would make their lives easier given C’s runner-up will face Group D’s top team, which will likely be Brazil. No. 45 Panama and No. 85 Bolivia shouldn’t pose much of a problem for the U.S. or No. 15 Uruguay. The United States opens competition against Bolivia on June 23 and faces Panama on June 27 before squaring off with Uruguay—which will likely determine the fate of the group. Uruguay is coming off of a mighty 4-nil win over Mexico on June 5 and possess a cast that could pose problems for the U.S., like Liverpool striker Darwin Núñez, Manchester United winger Facundo Pellistri, Tottenham midfielder Rodrigo Betancur, former Bracelona and Liverpool striker Luis Suárez, and world-class manager Marcelo Bielsa who loves to play on the attack. If I’m going off current run of form and quality of manager, it’s difficult to choose USA over Uruguay. I’m taking La Celeste to take Photo courtesy of CopaAmerica.com Can the U.S. win Group C? They face tough competition from a surging Uruguay group. 1C and USA as 2C, which should be a huge indictment against U.S. manager Gregg Berhalter. Group A: No. 1 Argentina, No. 32 Peru, No. 42 Chile, No. 49 Canada Aside from defending World Cup champions Argentina winning the group, this is an extra-difficult batch to predict. Each team has players that can provide a huge impact, like Peru with veteran forward André Carrillo, Chile with Inter Milan forward Alexis Sánchez, and Canada with Bayern Munich winger Alphonso Davies and Lille striker Jonathan David. In the end, I’m taking the Canadians’ star-power. Argentina takes 1B, Canada with 2B. Group B: No. 14 Mexico, No. 31 Ecuador, No. 54 Venezuela, No. 55 Jamaica Mexico enters its first tournament in years without veteran goalkeeper Memo Ochoa, but are still the favorites in the group with players like West Ham midfielder Edson Álvarez and shifty forward Alexis Vega. Jamaica brings talented players like West Ham striker Michail Antonio and Aston Villa winger Leon Bailey, but I’m leaning toward Ecuador’s talented cast of Bayern Leverkusen def’ender Piero Hincapié, Chelsea midfielder Moisés Caicedo, and the country’s All-Time top goalscorer, Enner Valencia. In the end, I’m taking Ecuador to take 1B and Mexico as runners up. Group D: No. 5 Brazil, No. 12 Colombia, No. 52 Costa Rica, No. 56 Paraguay This should be an easy prediction with a lot of disparity in the group; Brazil as 1D and Colombia as 2D. Quarterfinals predictions (1A) Argentina beats (2B) Mexico; (1B) Ecuador beats (2A) Canada; (1C) Uruguay beats (2D) Colombia; (1D) Brazil beats (2C) United States. articles.text: The school year is has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post lists our favorite 10 moments of the year. 1. Boys’ Water Polo’s NCS Championship Our top moment came before New Year on November 11 when Piedmont’s No. 4 seeded boys’ water polo team made history by winning the Division 2 North Coast Section title with a 10-8 win over No. 3 Alameda. Piedmont won the Western Alameda County Conference title in 2021 and 2022, but fell in the NCS semifinals in the two previous years against Marin Academy, finally getting over the hump with a 13-9 semis victory over the No. 1 ranked Wildcats. It marked the school’s first NCS title. 2. Baseball’s NCS & CIF run It was a historic 2024 season for Piedmont High’s baseball team. They won the WACC regular season first-place banner and reached the finals of the North Coast Section and the State NorCal tournaments. After falling as the No. 2 seed in the NCS postseason to No. 4 Justin-Siena on May 25, Piedmont battled to the CIF NorCal Championship as the No. 1 seed with a 13-1 win over No. 8 Capuchino on May 28, shutout No. 4 Colusa 5-0 in the semifinals on May 30, but lost 6-0 to Bradshaw Christian on June 1. 3. Football team wins Shoreline title On November 3, Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Shoreline Division title in a stress-inducing 29-26 win over Newark Memorial. It marked the first time the school has won a league banner since 2015, which was also the last time they won the Shoreline title. 2023 marked the return of the school’s 100 year-old varsity football program after it was shut down the previous year due to a lack of players. Going into 2024, the Highlanders were promoted to the Mission Division—the second tier of the WACC’s football pyramid. 4. Girls’ Lacrosse wins WACC title over Bishop O’Dowd The girls’ lacrosse team won its first WACC title since 2019 by beating rival Bishop O’Dowd 8-7 on April 26. Piedmont responded to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but quickly answered with goals by Friedie Schickedanz and two by Ruby Guzdar. Holding an 8-7 lead in the fourth quarter, the Highlanders killed over three minutes of clock to win the game. It was a big performance by goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter, recording 12 saves. 5. Natalia Martinez’s historic career 2023-24 was a historic season for senior guard Natalia Martinez, who graduates and is set to attend San Diego State. She concluded her high school career with 2,272 total points, including the school-record for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28. In a 40-point performance against San Leandro, Natalia went perfect 10/10 for 3-pointers, also creating a school record for hitting 100 percent beyond the arc for double-digit attempts. She is the Post’s first back-toback Athlete of the Year award winner. A top moment in sports includes the boys’ water polo team’s first North Coast Section championship on November 11. Pictured are Finn Burke helping to dunk coach Rik Krumins in the pool to celebrate. On November 3 Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Shoreline Championship against Newark Memorial. The baseball team advanced to the North Coast Section and the State regional playoffs and also played a game on March 23 at Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. 6. Sebastien Swain, the frosh phenom Freshman distance runner Sebastien Swain was a story, becoming our Freshman of the Year after qualifying for the State cross country meet in the fall and reaching the finals of the North Coast Section Meet of Champions in the spring track season. Swain was Piedmont’s only cross-country runner to qualify for the State meet on November 25 in Woodward Park. He finished 67th of 201 runners with a time of 16:41.3, earning him a selection on the 2023 All-State Freshman Team at the Division 4 level by Prep CalTrack. 7. Boys Basketball reaches NCS Finals The boys’ basketball team made it to the NCS Finals against No. 1 University where it lost 65-55 as the No. 3 seed. It marked the school’s first NCS Finals appearance since its D4 championship win in 2020. Reaching the championship meant Piedmont qualified for the CIF State Tournament as the No. 14 seed in the D3 bracket, falling to No. 3 Valley Christian in the opening round. articles.text: Violinist Jascha Heifetz Throughout history, great teachers have influenced public opinion. Sometimes they paid with their lives- Socrates, for example. We probably should include Jesus also. In America, we need to include Abraham Lincoln and Martin Luther King. This evening a friend treated us to a gondola ride on Lake Merritt, which gave me the opportunity to write this column. There were six musicians aboard making it the perfect opportunity to ask some probing questions. The noted pianist Gerald Robbins has been in town for a week. He has been regarded as an outstanding pianist for more than 60 years. What is particularly interesting is that he combines being an important soloist with being an important piano accompanist. Imagine being the pianist to the likes of Jascha Heifetz, Gregor Piatigorsky, Nathan Milstein, Rugierro Ricci and Aaron Rosand. All were the top echelon for the entire 20th century. What did Gerry learn from them? That’s what I asked him while we were gliding on the water at Lake Merritt. It turns out that Robbins was attuned to the highest levels of musical artistry from the beginning. Some people just know the secrets innately. In his case, he did learn a lot rubbing shoulders with genius and listening attentively. Here are some of the secrets of the masters which performers should know. It might be a good idea if listeners know some of the secrets also. 1) Always be prepared. Be sure to take the advice of those who have experience. 2) Always be diplomatic. You will get more gigs if people like you. 3) Be sure to position yourself in the best place when you perform. The truth is that it really does matter. We are fortunate to have videos that show where to position yourself. String players always ask themselves if they should have a really expensive instrument (such as a Stradivarius.) Yes, a Strad does help. But if you control the volume of your piano accompanist, you will always sound better. These are just a few of the secrets of the masters. Along the way it helps to be observant. Be an inspired performer. Inspiration gives us the ability to rise above the mundane problems of life. By doing so we can transport the listener to another world. Listeners should never accept mundane performances. Sometimes it’s a good idea to voice our opinion. Standing ovations are warranted when a performance is particularly good. Unfortunately, we yell “bravo!” for mediocrity. Jascha Heifetz was always very critical of his own playing. One time, he was not happy with his performance. The audience was standing up and yelling “bravo!” Heifetz said to himself “Please don’t give me a standing ovation. I didn’t play very well. I deserve to be booed.” Honesty like this is certainly rare. articles.text: Three popular art exhibitions at the Fine Arts museums of San Francisco will continue to be on view this summer. Irving Penn exhibit at de Young An exhibition featuring the work of widely-recognized photographer Irving Penn is on view at the de Young museum in San Francisco through July 21. Penn is Vogue Magazine’s longest-standing contributor, and he became the most influential fashion photographer in the postwar era. Known for his use of neutral backgrounds, he emphasized models’ personalities through their gestures and expressions. The exhibition includes 175 photographs, spanning every period of Penn’s nearly 70-year career and ranging from early documentary scenes, celebrity portraits, and workers with the tools of their trades to abstract nudes and fashion studies. This presentation also features a special section of photographs made during Penn’s 1967 trip to San Francisco, where Penn captures the iconic “Summer of Love.” Included are his portraits of bona fide hippies, members of the Hells Angels Motorcycle Club, and local rock bands the Grateful Dead and Big Brother and the Holding Company. To learn more, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/irving-penn?mc_ cid=20 ab 0f 52d7& a mp;mc _ eid=573801a180. Fashion exhibit at de Young Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style features iconic collections of 20th and 21stcentury women’s fashion in the United States and the Bay Area. The exhibition includes over 100 pieces, some loaned by local collectors of haute couture, and is the first major presentation of the museum’s own costume collection. A wide range of fashion is represented from French dressmakers to Japanese avant-garde designers. Designs by Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, Christopher John Rogers, Comme des Garçons, Rei Kawakubo, Kei Ninomiya, Junya Watanabe, Yohji Yamamoto and Rodarte are on display. “These garments echo the evolving urban landscape of San Francisco, a city populated by structures that push the confines of modern architecture, likewise made by advanced engineering and with state-of-the-art industrial materials,” said Laura Camerlengo, curator of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Fashioning San Francisco is on display through August. Visit https://www.famsf.org/exhibitions/fashioning-san-francisco to learn more. Japanese prints exhibit at Legion of Honor Legion of Honor in San Francisco’s newest exhibition Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World is on view through August 18. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade, highlighting the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period marks when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of feudal military rule in the Asian country. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art and especially printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked both pre and postMeiji era. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints. A patron views Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style at de Young Museum. articles.text: A few backstory comments: Going in Style was first made in 1979 and starred George Burns, Art Carney and Lee Strasberg. It was well received then, as was the 1993 “Grumpy Old Men,” starring the incomparable Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon. Cantankerous old men at loose ends, seated on a generic park bench sharing their mildly cynical commentary on life as it passes them by, is a theme that Hollywood has often visited and revisited. In the current incarnation, Going in Style has an A-list trio of actors – Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Alan Arkin – in what proves to be a familiar yet satisfactory story about three geezers, Willie (Freeman), Joe (Caine) and Albert (Arkin), who are all facing their end-game while exigent circumstances bear down, forcing them to transcend old age and retirement with more than a sigh and a shrug of the shoulders. As they soon learn, the company they spent 30 years serving has just been outsourced and in doing so cancelled their pensions. Willie is also suffering from renal failure, a fact he is keeping to himself. It is a truism that when you’re living what will likely be the last full decade of your life, you are reminded daily that your body will offer one small (or large) betrayal after the next. When Albert is reminded that life is short, he says something akin to, “tell me something I don’t know.” As well, Joe has just learned his house is in foreclosure (no pension means no house). While in the bank, asking the manager what that exactly that will mean, the place is held up. The robbers abscond with serious cash and, Joe notices the holdup guys pull off the job with essentially no harm no foul (well, there is the question of 2 million bucks now missing). It’s at this point when Going in Style could have been the movie it should have been. At least in act one and perhaps part of act two. The park bench conversations could have dealt with the reality of what it means to live in a culture where oldsters are pretty much assigned to the cheap seats. Ours is a culture where if you are in your 80s, life is happening on the field of play, observable, at times a bit confusing or disconcerting, especially since it seems to be moving with the speed of a double play or someone trying to steal home plate. And it can often feel just a bit (or a lot) out of reach. Their halcyon days are now recalled while looking in the rearview mirror. What the dynamic trio does, instead of mulling over their existential plight, is decide to plan a bank caper, inspired by Joe after observing his own bank being held up. So the three old guys, who are each a delight to watch as they keep this average story moving right along, work out their own heist (same bank), right down to a gnats eyebrow. articles.text: Film contains top talent of actors Pedro Almodovar: two Oscars, six BAFTAs (British), nine Goyas (Spanish), honorary doctorates from Harvard and Oxford, and 40 years of working at the craft of filmmaking, his chosen a medium which has allowed him to repeatedly examine the richness of the human condition. In his most recent film, Pain and Glory, he has created a spare narrative, never stark, never confused by vanity, but one that is close-to-the-bone subtle and nuanced, offered as auto-fiction and written and directed by Almodovar, who is now in his 70s. The lead character, Salvador Mallo, is a world-famous writer and filmmaker named Salvador Mallo, superbly portrayed by Antonio Banderas who is a ringer for Almodovar, down to the clothes he wears, his graying beard and spiky hair. The setting, almost exclusively, is Mallo’s Madrid apartment (recreated from Almodovar’s own apartment, with his personal art on the walls). Mallo is a man who is aging badly and feels betrayed by his body. And just to be clear about the vagaries of that betrayal, at the outset of the film, using animation, Mallo, in voice over, lists the afflictions that plague him: sciatica, depression, tinnitus, migraines, insomnia, a fused back, a throat that abruptly closes causing uncontrollable coughing, all buffered by alcohol and meds. Professionally, he refuses to write because physically he cannot direct what he might create. He wonders if he will ever work again, a voiced lament to a longago collaborator, actor Alberto Crespo (Asier Etxeandia), a man he has not seen for some 30 years, and with whom he smokes, for the first time, heroin; anything to relieve the pain. And it is when he falls into a heroin-induced reverie and dreams about his childhood and his mother, Jacinta (Penelope Cruz), he remembers an apartment-like cave they lived in when the family left their village and the underground home being filled with his mother’s love. In truth, Pain and Glory is a kind of reverie, often dream-like when Mallo, who lives like a hermit, and is only visited or rescued by loyal women who satellite his life while caring for him. In is a series of revelations, often steeped in regret, his story now a soft lament. Keep in mind that this film is told by an unreliable narrator (Mallo/Almodovar), and is framed by a spectrum of startling primary colors that belie Mallo’s condition and viewpoint. Deep reds enter almost every scene, often coordinated with his shirts and the window coverings; rainbows of colors are everywhere, in his flashbacks and in his daily life, a seeming contradiction. The exposition, in an unexpected way, is uplifting, for Mallo still refuses to yield. He even writes as if that very act is one of self-deception, yet the words are his own. Pain and Glory is, to be sure, a quiet meditation on aging and the physical betrayal that accompanies that experience. For Mallo, his physical pain is a reminder of a reality from which he can find no exit. He acknowledges that he is in the autumn of his life, heading toward winter. His dreams – his mother, of her washing clothes by a river, singing with the other village women – are of spring. This is his life, wistfully told, tenderly offered, a nexus of pain and glory while he hopes that still there is work ahead. A fact that is demonstrated so eloquently in this film. Pain and Glory. Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine, Alan Arkin – the dynamic trio in Going in Style By Chris Honoré A few backstory comments: Going in Style was first made in 1979 and starred George Burns, Art Carney and Lee Strasberg. It was well received then, as was the 1993 “Grumpy Old Men,” starring the incomparable Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon. Cantankerous old men at loose ends, seated on a generic park bench sharing their mildly cynical commentary on life as it passes them by, is a theme that Hollywood has often visited and revisited. In the current incarnation, Going in Style has an A-list trio of actors – Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Alan Arkin – in what proves to be a familiar yet satisfactory story about three geezers, Willie (Freeman), Joe (Caine) and Albert (Arkin), who are all facing their end-game while exigent circumstances bear down, forcing them to transcend old age and retirement with more than a sigh and a shrug of the shoulders. As they soon learn, the company they spent 30 years serving has just been outsourced and in doing so cancelled their pensions. Willie is also suffering from renal failure, a fact he is keeping to himself. It is a truism that when you’re living what will likely be the last full decade of your life, you are reminded daily that your body will offer one small (or large) betrayal after the next. When Albert is reminded that life is short, he says something akin to, “tell me something I don’t know.” As well, Joe has just learned his house is in foreclosure (no pension means no house). While in the bank, asking the manager what that exactly that will mean, the place is held up. The robbers abscond with serious cash and, Joe notices the holdup guys pull off the job with essentially no harm no foul (well, there is the question of 2 million bucks now missing). It’s at this point when Going in Style could have been the movie it should have been. At least in act one and perhaps part of act two. The park bench conversations could have dealt with the reality of what it means to live in a culture where oldsters are pretty much assigned to the cheap seats. Ours is a culture where if you are in your 80s, life is happening on the field of play, observable, at times a bit confusing or disconcerting, especially since it seems to be moving with the speed of a double play or someone trying to steal home plate. And it can often feel just a bit (or a lot) out of reach. Their halcyon days are now recalled while looking in the rearview mirror. What the dynamic trio does, instead of mulling over their existential plight, is decide to plan a bank caper, inspired by Joe after observing his own bank being held up. So the three old guys, who are each a delight to watch as they keep this average story moving right along, work out their own heist (same bank), right down to a gnats eyebrow. The only question left to answer has nothing to do with their geezer-hood, but the how of planning a crime that will allow them to later enjoy the spoils of the robbery. Of course, going to jail at 80 is the equivalent of a life sentence and to be avoided at all cost. That proves to be their challenge. Anyway, there are three reasons to see Going in Style, and they are Freeman, Caine and Arkin. They are treasures and, to use a cliché, could read the menu at their favorite movie diner (where they are loathe to tip) and make it sound interesting. Going in Style. Directed by Zach Braft. articles.text: Disney’s animated Oscar nominated Big Hero 6 will appeal to an audience of tweens and newbie teens. The narrative, a derivative of Marvel’s superhero characters, features 14-year-old Hiro Hamada (Ryan Potter), a nerdy, robotics obsessed kid. He lives in the futuristic Asian-like city of San Fransokyo, where he hangs out with a cohort of extraordinary friends: GoGo Tanago (Jamie Chung), Wasabi (Damon Wayans, Jr.), and Honey Lemon (Genesis Rodriguez). Hiro, who graduated from high school at the age of 14, spends his days submerged in techie stuff. At night, however, he engages in illegal robotic fight games. His older brother, Tadashi (Daniel Henney), worries about Hiro’s night-time antics, so with the encouragement of both Hiro’s aunt, Cass (Maya Rudolph), and Tadashi, he agrees to visit the cutting-edge Institute of San Fransokyo. They hope to influence the young prodigy to give up his underground exploits, and come to the realization that there is a world beyond his own niche of homegrown high tech stuff. A scene from Big Hero 6 As it turns out, the visit to the university proves a success. Hiro, captivated, meets kindred spirits, sees advanced labs, and meets the distinguished Professor Callaghan (James Cromwell), head of robotics, and the inventor of a medical bot, Baymax (Scott Adsit), programed to care for his charge. It eventually becomes Hiro’s sidekick of sorts. Of course, there is a sudden turn of events, which impacts Hiro and his buds, and they soon discover that as a result, their lives have been turned upside down. What occurs? Well, they unexpectedly discover an ominous, dangerous plot that pulls the gang into a harrowing adventure that is brimming with fun, action, and imaginative science (an example being a swarm of buzzing microbots). Older kids, tweens and teens will find Big Hero 6 a compelling watch, and Hiro an interesting role model. The world of high tech/A.I. is upon us. Hiro is already there. Big Hero 6. articles.text: I found Gifted engaging and watchable. The cast – a wonderful ensemble – is excellent, especially the performance of McKenna Grace as Mary, a 7-year-old math prodigy. She is a small powerhouse of emotion and a perfect contrast to Chris Evans as her laconic uncle Frank. As it is quickly revealed, Frank has raised Mary since infancy (her mother committed suicide) and the two have formed an unshakable bond. He has accomplished this while living in a shack in Florida, supporting the two of them by repairing boats. He also has the help of a neighbor, Roberta, played perfectly by Octavia Spencer. Their nicely balanced lives are abruptly disrupted when Frank decides that Mary should attend first grade at the nearest school. His thought is that she needs to learn to live among other kids. Mary votes for continued homeschooling. As does Roberta. What Mary’s teacher, Bonnie (Jenny Slate), is not prepared for is that Mary is a math genius and bored to distraction (and crankiness) by the simple rote learning. At a young age Mary is already doing quadratic equations. Frank is called in for a parent-teacher conference with Bonnie and school administrators who argue that Mary belongs in a gifted school where she will be challenged. Frank, wanting her to experience the world as it is, disagrees. And it’s then that Frank’s estranged mother, Evelyn (Lindsay Duncan), a wealthy Bostonian, enters their lives, bringing her high-priced attorney and a suit for custody. She has decided that Mary needs a far different environment than the one provided by Frank. It becomes clear that Gifted is a child custody story where both Mary and Frank are put under the court’s microscope while Evelyn is relentless. Throughout the film the interactions between Mary and Frank are priceless. And the courtroom drama is filled with tension as Mary’s fate hangs in the balance. What is agreed to, is not what you might expect, and it all has to do with Mary’s one-eyed cat named Fred. Gifted is simple and direct, with enough emotional horsepower to bring a tear or two. This may be Chris Evans’ best movie to date. And McKenna Grace delivers a tour de force performance as Mary and carries the film from the first scene. Gifted. Directed by Marc Webb. articles.text: Oakland Zoo hosted its third annual Bear Camp event to celebrate National Black Bear Day on Saturday, June 1. Guests watched the Zoo’s black bears destroy a demonstration campsite set up inside the habitat, and learned how to be beware while in bear country. U.S. Forest Service Rangers and Smokey the Bear joined in to watch the bears explore a tent and picnic table. As guests said hello to Smokey and wished him a happy 80th birthday, they got to talk with the Rangers and learn about fire safety, just in time for summer. In June 2017, when they were just cubs, this family of bears entered an older woman’s home, and the mother bear injured the homeowner who was trying to chase them out. After this incident, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife moved the bear family to Oakland Zoo. Not all human-wildlife conflict situations have this positive outcome. The Zoo urges the public to join them in Taking Action for Wildlife to minimize these conflicts. The most common humanbear conflicts involve unsecured garbage and food. articles.text: If you are like me, the differences between all those buildings with prominent columns on them has always been a little unclear. Maybe today we can begin to sort it out. First, we go back to the Greeks. Their architecture was simpler, characterized by closely spaced columns because their era did not have the spanning capability of the arch. Along came the Romans, who in addition to borrowing heavily from the Greeks, were beneficiaries of the invention of concrete which allowed vaults, domes and arches, leading to a different, more developed architecture. Although the Greek and Roman civilizations were about 1000 years apart at their peaks, in our era the architecture they produced has been conventionally lumped together as Classical Architecture. This Classical Architecture was, and indeed is, pretty amazing. Well thought out with mathematically calculated proportions that are pleasing to the eye and mind, they seem to form a natural part of the universal order. Certainly they have endured over the centuries, having been “revived” numerous times. As this country was being formed in the late 1700’s, most of the new construction was strongly influenced by settlers from Europe, especially from England, to which we were attached as colonies. At that time there was a Classical Revival in vogue in Europe. It appeared on this side of the pond as well, and was the start of our Colonial Architecture style. Fast forward 100 years of style preference upswings and downswings to the Centennial Exhibition of 1876 in Chicago – America’s first World’s Fair. With 10 million visitors viewing the pervasive Classical style architecture of the fair developed principally by the architect Daniel Burnham, America was exposed and reawakPhots and Sketches by Will Adams The classical orders are the various sub-styles of Classical Architecture that evolved over the centuries. They are most easily identified by the column capitals, but include the whole of the building – proportions, profiles, and detailing. This seemingly timeless aesthetic still remains a source for various design styles (including some contemporary styles) in the 21st century. On the spectrum of revival styles, these impressive Piedmont homes tend towards Classical Revival (or Neoclassical). That is because they utilize the classical characteristics of large porticos (covered, columned entries), tall columns and classical orders (note the Ionic and Corinthian columns). They also tend towards formality because of their symmetry – the entry in the center of the building mass with the same balanced facades on each side.

articles.text: High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. It’s filled with houses now, but 130 years ago the United States Experimental Silk Culture Station was raising silkworms and promoting silkworm culture there. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk-producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Silkworms ate their own weight 50 times over during their fast growing life. Women harvested the leaves, chopped them up and fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s, silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. After six years, the Piedmont silk station failed to make a profit despite federal aid. The government stopped its appropriations in 1891, and the silk farm closed four years later. It was Piedmont’s only industry. Today, there are still mulberries in Piedmont. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. Their logo is a leaf with silkworm bites. Mulberry trees were also planted at the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Field in memory of the role they played in Piedmont’s early history. For more on Piedmont’s history and the Piedmont Historical Society, visit the website: Piedmonthistorical.org. A wood rack with cocoons is at his feet, with more racks on the top shelf. The girls are preparing fresh silkworm trays with screens and mulberry leaves. The shelves behind them are filled with trays of silkworms and mulberry leaves. The machine at the right foreground chops mulberry leaves before they are fed to the silkworms. The sign reads “U.S. Experimental Silk Culture Station, Oakland Cal.”

pages.text: Wednesday, June 19, 2024 27 The History of Piedmont Piedmont’s silk farm – it’s all about mulberry leaves By Gail G. Lombardi High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. It’s filled with houses now, but 130 years ago the United States Experimental Silk Culture Station was raising silkworms and promoting silkworm culture there. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk-producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” By 1885, the mulberry grove was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Silkworms ate their own weight 50 times over during their fast growing life. Women harvested the leaves, chopped them up and fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s, silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. After six years, the Piedmont silk station failed to make a profit despite federal aid. The government stopped its appropriations in 1891, and the silk farm closed four years later. It was Piedmont’s only industry. Today, there are still mulberries in Piedmont. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. Their logo is a leaf with silkworm bites. Mulberry trees were also planted at the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Field in memory of the role they played in Piedmont’s early history. The family had it appraised at $750; but the New Orleans auctioneer valuation was between $1,200 and $1,800. Its catalog blurb played up “the fine antique gilt frame.” Gallery owner Robert Simon of New York City was tipped off by an associate Alexander Parish, an art-picker whose expertise is scouring the internet for potential finds, shared the hope of connecting the work to a Leonardo disciple. When Simon examined the work in person, he deemed it a wreck with “wormy panel, cradled [lattice support backing], badly overpainted, and scraped with a sharp tool.” That said, he recognized the oil-on-panel looked to be of Renaissance vintage and noted that parts were skillfully done, such as the figure’s left-side curls, the orb, and right hand in blessing: also “it was dirty, dark, and gloomy.” They were stunned to win the bid at $1,000. The Salvator Mundi controversy The art-dealer consortium turned to Dianne Modestini, a New York University research professor and renowned restorer. Dianne’s first reaction was that Christ’s face looked like a “clown mask” and she recommended a junior restorer, but after a few sample-test cleanings, she changed her mind. They engaged a Madrid specialist, Monica Griesbach, who disengaged the painting’s backing, and “the entire painting came apart in her hands breaking into seven pieces.” She spent six months reassembling the painting – mending with adhesive and tiny wood slivers. The restoration was slow and painstaking and took six years, while Simon researched for authentication. Once they concluded it was Leonardo’s work, the job was to build consensus among art historians. Opinions were far from unanimous. The big breakthrough happened in 2011 when the National Gallery in London accepted Salvator Mundi in the Leonardo da Vinci: from Milan show. Among European art extravaganzas, perhaps the most popular was Leonardo da Vinci at the Louvre, a retrospective celebrating 500 years since the artist’s death and showing off the artist’s remarkable works. Twice the painting’s unveilings were abruptly canceled without explanation. Paintings by the enigmatic Leonardo are among the rarest of Old Masters. Except for two in private hands – most are owned by museums. The Louvre owns five, including Mona Lisa. Italy owns three, counting the ruined Last Supper. The U.S. has one. How many Leonardo paintings exist remains in dispute, but the number is believed to be fewer than 20. Though unquestionably one of the greatest painters known to the world, based upon the time invested in the paintings, he was not prolific. He frequently abandoned works when his interest waned or was diverted. His painting was slow, and he clung to works to reach perfection. Consider the Mona Lisa (La Joconde in French), a painting he carted around Italy and France to his dying day. Leonardo’s philosophy was that money in abundance does not end well. Renaissance Man Born in the Florence countryside in 1452, Leonardo’s gifts manifested early. By age 14, he was apprenticed to Andrea del Verrocchio’s workshop, where his formal schooling trailed off and self-study bloomed. He became immersed in languages, natural sciences, history, philosophy, and mathematics – disciplines that substantially informed his art. Much of what is known about his polymathic genius is in his notebooks – thousands of pages of densely inscribed notes and drawings that have survived and were displayed at the Louvre. Leonardo’s longest patronage was with Duke Ludovico Sforza of Milan – where he especially thrived, not just as painter and sculptor. He was an engineer and architect, especially for military charting and weaponry. As First Painter, he designed theatre and opera sets.
